Hours after the Obama administration
announced the criminal conviction
of
Credit Suisse
on Monday evening, the bank’s chief executive, Brady W. Dougan,
publicly reassured Wall Street
that the punishment would not do much damage to his firm. The conviction, he said on a conference call, would not cause “any material impact on our operational or business capabilities.”
And in many ways, that was exactly the outcome that the American authorities desired.
Related Links
Timeline
|
Documents
Credit Suisse Investors Shrug Off Tax Plea (May 20, 2014)
The Justice Department and bank regulators had worked hard to find a careful balance. When
Credit Suisse
pleaded guilty to the crime of aiding tax evasion, prosecutors did not want the action to lead to repercussions that could destabilize the bank or the wider financial system.
So far, that arrangement seems to have been achieved. The question, however, is whether it amounts to justice.
The United States attorney general,
Eric H. Holder Jr.
, believes that it does. “This case shows that no financial institution, no matter its size or global reach, is above the law,” he said in a statement on Monday about Credit Suisse’s guilty plea.
In some respects, Credit Suisse is definitely being punished. The conviction is a stubborn stain on Credit Suisse’s name. The bank finds itself
in the company of corporate felons
that include
Drexel Burnham Lambert
, the ethically challenged Wall Street firm, and Arthur Andersen,
Enron
’s auditor. (Both firms died in part because the government pursued tough measures against them.)
In addition, the
$2.6 billion in penalties that Credit Suisse has agreed to pay
is not an insignificant sum. In fact, some legal experts say that figure most likely far exceeds the amount of unpaid taxes in the disputed accounts. In this case, unlike so many others, the American authorities actually pursued individuals who they believed were guilty of wrongdoing. It indicted eight Credit Suisse employees, obtaining guilty pleas from two so far.
And a convicted bank faces a severe response from law enforcement agencies if it does more wrongdoing, according to an official in the Justice Department who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “Felons almost always face even harsher punishments if they reoffend,” the person said. “And given its status, the bank has to be concerned not just about U.S. regulators and prosecutors, but also regulators around the world.”
Still, the settlement left some critics of big banks disappointed for what it didn’t do.
It did not produce the names of people whose accounts may have been used for tax evasion. Senator
Carl Levin
, Democrat of Michigan, who led a congressional investigation of Credit Suisse’s tax-related activities, said that he supported the Justice Department’s actions against the bank, but added: “It is a mystery to me why the U.S. government didn’t require as part of the agreement that the bank cough up some of the names of the U.S. clients with secret Swiss bank accounts.”
The bank’s most senior executives, including Mr. Dougan, got to keep their jobs, leading another senator to criticize the government’s settlement. “Nor does the plea deal hold any officers, directors or key executives individually accountable for wrongdoing, raising the question of whether it will sufficiently deter similar misconduct in the future,” Senator
John McCain
, Republican of Arizona, said in a statement.
A conviction may in theory prompt trading partners or clients to stop doing business with the bank, but Mr. Dougan suggested on Tuesday that they were not withdrawing. Even the bank’s public statement on the conviction was somewhat tepid. In the statement Credit Suisse released on Monday, Mr. Dougan’s comments did not contain the words “guilty” or “conviction.” Instead, he merely said, “We deeply regret the past misconduct that led to this settlement.”
“If there are no consequences from a criminal conviction, they are just dumbing down a criminal conviction,” Rebel A. Cole, a professor of finance at
DePaul University
, said.
Still, real-world considerations usually make it impossible to achieve perfect justice — and the Credit Suisse case has gray areas.
In some respects, it was just as much a fight between the American and Swiss governments as a battle between Credit Suisse and United States law enforcement authorities. The Justice Department wanted Credit Suisse to provide the names of clients who were potential tax evaders, but the Swiss government did not grant an exemption to Swiss law that in theory would have allowed the bank to do that. The Justice Department nevertheless pressed ahead with its criminal case against the bank.
But the issue of the client names wasn’t the only reason the Justice Department pursued a criminal conviction. Its statement of facts laid out areas unrelated to the names in which Credit Suisse’s management could have been more cooperative.
The bank did not retain certain documents, it failed to interview potentially culpable bankers before they left the firm, and it did not start an internal inquiry until 2011, which was many months after the American authorities began to step up their scrutiny of Swiss banks for tax evasion.
“Among other things, prosecutors are required to consider the company’s compliance program and the quality of its cooperation in determining how to proceed,” Daniel W. Levy, a principal at the law firm McKool Smith, said. “Here, the government thought that Credit Suisse’s compliance program and cooperation were subpar.”
Given the lackluster cooperation, the American authorities may have had grounds to demand tougher punishments than they did. And if they had threatened, or applied, stricter actions, they might have been able to get the names of the potential tax evaders, possibly allowing them to solve the underlying crimes, which is one aim of good justice.
If Credit Suisse suffers no real business consequences as a result of its conviction, banking regulators may have to get creative and devise more painful sanctions that are not life-threatening.
A tough-but-not-fatal measure may soon emerge from the office of Benjamin M. Lawsky, the New York State superintendent of financial services. The agency is preparing to accept a guilty plea from the French bank
BNP Paribas
for suspected sanctions violations. In that case, Mr. Lawsky might decide to temporarily suspend the bank’s ability to transfer money through New York for foreign customers. That would most likely hurt, depending on its terms, but it would almost certainly not prove fatal.
Another partial punishment might be to temporarily ban a Wall Street firm from trading with the
Federal Reserve
. Banks that have this special role are called primary dealers, and trade mostly in government bonds with the
Federal Reserve Bank of New York
as part of the Fed’s efforts to manage monetary policy.
According to its operating policy, the
New York Fed
“expects a primary dealer to maintain a robust compliance program, including procedures to identify and mitigate legal, regulatory, financial, and reputational risks.” These are the sorts of risks that Credit Suisse failed to manage properly in the tax evasion case.
The Credit Suisse subsidiary that is a primary dealer remains in that role.
“We considered this matter and decided, in light of all the facts and consistent with the standards set out in our operating policy for primary dealers, to continue the counterparty relationship,” a New York Fed official said. “It is important to note that regulators made the collective decision to allow the firm and its subsidiaries to continue its operations, including in the markets in which we transact.”

LEAVE it to a native New Yorker who hasn’t lived here in 53 years to still know the best place to go.
Garry Marshall, director of the movies “Pretty Woman,” “Beaches” and “The Princess Diaries,” who also created the television series “Happy Days,” “Laverne and Shirley” and “Mork and Mindy,” is from the Grand Concourse in the Bronx. He loved his old neighborhood and never lost his delight in its easy camaraderie. So much so that when he shoots a movie, people say he doesn’t direct it as much as throw it. When I arrived at the elegant yet warmly appointed
bar
at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel on Central Park South — his choice — I began to see what that meant.
Mr. Marshall, who turns 80 in November, ordered an anisette, two ice cubes — as a cocktail — and called over his friend
Norman Bukofzer
, the head barman. Mr. Marshall likes him so much he cast him in his latest film, “New Year’s Eve.”
“Tell her your line,” he instructed, first giving me the setup, a character saying that New York City is a dangerous place. Mr. Bukofzer struck a pose. “You ever been to Newark?” he growled. Mr. Marshall laughed. “Four takes, he did it,” he said. When Mr. Bukofzer walked away, Mr. Marshall said: “He should be in the business. He knows everybody.”
Perhaps, but when it comes to networking, no one tops Mr. Marshall. He’s been working longer and harder than most people in any business, starting in 1959, when he wrote for Joey Bishop and then for Jack Paar on “The Tonight Show” before moving on to “The Dick Van Dyke Show” and “The Lucy Show.” He produced “The Odd Couple,” with Jack Klugman and Tony Randall. And on “Murphy Brown,” he played the head of the network.
Mr. Marshall is back in New York to direct a new play, “
Billy & Ray
,” by Mike Bencivenga, starring Vincent Kartheiser (Pete Campbell on “Mad Men”) and featuring Sophie von Haselberg, otherwise known as Bette Midler’s daughter. “I remember on the set of ‘Beaches,’ holding her hand and saying, ‘Let’s go see what Mommy’s doing now,’ ” Mr. Marshall recalled.

“Billy & Ray” tells the story of how Raymond Chandler (Larry Pine) and Billy Wilder (Mr. Kartheiser) wrote the classic film noir “Double Indemnity.” The play was first produced by the
Falcon Theater
in Burbank, Calif., which is owned by Mr. Marshall and run by his daughter Kathleen. It begins previews at the Vineyard Theater in Manhattan on Wednesday.
Mr. Marshall made a point of saying that Ms. Von Haselberg had auditioned through the Falcon independently, even though he is famous for casting his family and friends in everything, perhaps most memorably his sister Penny Marshall in “Laverne and Shirley.” Working with relatives can be hazardous: Mr. Marshall made his father, Tony, a producer on that show, and one week, Tony decided to withhold his daughter’s $25,000 paycheck. She had been “fresh” to him, he informed his son. Mr. Marshall intervened.

Mr. Bukofzer told us that the chef wanted to bring over some hors d’oeuvres. Mr. Marshall regarded him glumly. He was already picking at a fruit plate, and we had a dinner reservation at Redeye Grill, owned by another friend, Shelly Fireman, a fellow alumnus of DeWitt Clinton High School in the Bronx. Eating is not one of Mr. Marshall’s strong suits, he kept insisting. As a child, he had dangerous allergies — mustard could stop his breathing — and he still views many foods as potential enemies.
“Vinegar, horseradish, walnut oil,” he lamented. “One of my worst words is ‘drizzle.’ It’s the stuff they put in that you can’t see. My wife and my assistant, Heather, taste first to see what’s in a sauce. I should be a king! But I’m constantly blindsided by food. When I was a teenager, I could never put mustard on a hot dog. So I watched what the girls ate. If it was mustard, I didn’t want to hit on them. Maybe if a cute girl didn’t eat the mustard, I could kiss her.”
“I have a boring diet, but I’m happy,” he went on. “The new stuff, dandelion greens, Japanese turnips?” He shuddered and, pointing to his distended left cheek, added, “Mouth cancer also doesn’t help.” He received the diagnosis before directing “New Year’s Eve” in 2011.
But he is still a handsome devil. He appeared this season in an episode of “Two and a Half Men,” and Betty White has asked him to play a boyfriend on “Hot in Cleveland.” He was also in an episode of “Louie,” with Jay Leno and Jerry Seinfeld. “When Louis C.K. called, I had to ask my son who he was, and he told me he was a very big deal,” Mr. Marshall said, amused. “He was very nice.”
The chef presented the hors d’oeuvres: almost raw tuna, goat cheese, foie gras and lobster. “Is there vinegar?” Mr. Marshall asked suspiciously. The chef looked puzzled. “There is some acid,” he allowed. Once he left, Mr. Marshall opined darkly, “They say acid, but they mean vinegar.” He ate the foie gras and goat cheese and lived.
Despite having his right knee replaced eight weeks ago, Mr. Marshall grabbed his cane and insisted we walk the few blocks to Redeye. I told him I had read both his memoirs, “
Wake Me When It’s Funny
” and “
My Happy Days in Hollywood
,” written with his daughter Lori, and remarked on how positive he remained, especially in such a tough business.
“With cancer, I was not so positive,” he said at the table, sipping another anisette. “I thought I would never get better.” After radiation treatments, he shot “New Year’s Eve” in a brutal New York winter and contracted walking pneumonia. Once he recovered, Mr. Marshall’s wife of 51 years, Barbara, a former intensive-care nurse, insisted he go back to work. “I told her: ‘I can’t do a movie. I froze on ‘New Year’s Eve,’ ” Mr. Marshall said. “But the weather is always good in the theater.”
Our first course arrived, the miso matzo ball soup with shiitake mushrooms. It was delicious, a clever hybrid of Japanese and Jewish. Everyone thinks you’re Jewish, I told Mr. Marshall, né Masciarelli. He laughed. “We’re from the Bronx,” he said. “We’re all the same.”
We shared guacamole before he polished off a Dover sole with lemon butter sauce and creamed spinach. He ordered cheesecake for dessert, which he doused with a small pitcher of chocolate sauce. He ate, as my mother would say, like a horse.
When Mr. Marshall produced “Happy Days,” he had a basketball court on the Paramount lot and a malted milk machine in his office. He still loves sports and plays in a senior softball league, where he will return in November, once his knee has healed.
“After softball, we go to Denny’s, where we get a deal,” he told me. “I get an Oreo shake. And the soup is $2! The whole team eats.”

Neighbors and Strangers
Readers responded to the
special issue
of Dec. 9 examining Mars and our fascination with it:
TO THE EDITOR:
In the 1960s when I was part of the team flying the remotely controlled balloon telescope Stratoscope II, we looked at the results of balloon-borne science and said, you can either bring a man back alive or bring scientific results. The Darwinian process has designed humans for the surface of the Earth, and we cannot change that. In contrast, when we make devices for space we use intelligent design. If only we could redesign ourselves for space. We would not make humans with all the genetic garbage of the history of life, but creatures that could exchange information efficiently, hibernate for long journeys and have multiple copies of information so that cosmic ray damage could be mitigated. Who wants to be a blob of carbon-rich material that used to be alive on a planet that may or may not have had life of its own? Life offers us a chance to know by being. Just to be is not a life activity.
Neville Woolf
Tucson
The writer is professor emeritus of astronomy, Steward Observatory, University of Arizona.

What Happens in the End
TO THE EDITOR:
Re “
Hoping for a Good Death
” (Dec. 2): Elizabeth Reis’s thoughtful and sensitive piece epitomizes the dilemma patients and families face with increasing frequency in an era of extraordinary medical capabilities. More than 50 years ago, Jean Rostand, a French biologist and philosopher, wrote, “Science has made gods of us before we are even worthy of being men.” His prescient remark goes to the heart of certain problematic aspects of modern medical practice.
Some physicians seem unable to resist the technological imperative. (To someone with a hammer everything looks like a nail). If we know how to do it then we must do it. But it is not always wise to perceive death as an enemy that must be defeated — or held at bay indefinitely — without considering the cost to patients and their families.
Peter Rogatz, M.D.

KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Bob Dustman works on the fourth floor of Kauffman Stadium, by the elevator near the broadcast booths, his post for 11 seasons. He has a television in the lobby to watch the
Royals
play, and decades of memories around him on the walls.
One of the photographs, in black and white, was snapped just after the pivotal moment of the 1985 World Series. Reggie Jackson — moonlighting for ABC Sports — has his arm around the Royals’ manager, Dick Howser, while interviewing Dane Iorg, whose single had just brought home the tying and winning runs in the bottom of the ninth inning to beat the
St. Louis Cardinals
in Game 6.
The next night, the Royals won their only championship in a rout.
“It was the I-70 World Series,” Dustman said, “so there were a lot of pockets of red that dropped out as the game went on.”
Dustman, 81, saw those final World Series games — the last postseason appearances for the Royals until now — from the upper deck high above third base, a few rows from the top. The family also saw two games in the American League Championship Series.
“They were trailing the Angels around the first of September, and everybody thought they didn’t have a chance,” said Dustman’s son, Greg, now 53. “That’s how we got a lot of tickets — we had to mail away for them, and not a lot of people did. They didn’t want to tie up their money in tickets they wouldn’t even need.”
These Royals, likewise, took a while to convince their fans. Just as in 1985, they did not establish a winning record for good until July. Neither team clinched a playoff berth until the final weekend of the regular season.
Another similarity could reveal itself this week. These Royals, like those, could play their cross-state rival in the World Series.
Both championship series went dark on Monday: the National League for a travel day, the A.L. for a rainout. The Royals did not practice outside, which meant none of them were trapped under the tarpaulin covering the infield. Twenty-nine years ago on Monday, to the day, the Cardinals were not as lucky.
Their speedy leadoff man, Vince Coleman, fractured his knee when a mechanical tarp rolled over his leg as he left the Busch Stadium field before a game in the N.L.C.S. That freak injury did not stop the Cardinals from winning the pennant, and the 2014 Cardinals hope that another star’s injury does not doom them, either.
Catcher Yadier Molina strained an oblique muscle on a swing in Game 2 on Sunday. The Cardinals won the game to even their series against the Giants, 1-1, but oblique injuries like Molina’s often take weeks to heal.
In 1985, the Cardinals nearly overcame the loss of Coleman before falling apart with a 1-0 lead and three outs to go in Game 6. After the Royals’ unlikely winning rally — with a missed call at first base, a fallen foul pop, a passed ball, a bunt, an intentional walk and three singles — and their Game 7 triumph, they have had bragging rights for decades here.

“But that team’s special, and Kansas City’s always had that to hold on to.”
Dustman holds on to it literally. That summer, he had brought a baseball to a Photo Day event on the field and gotten 10 or 15 signatures. After the season, he brought the ball to a banquet and had a few more players sign it.
Just like that, Dustman had autographs of more than half the members of a championship team, all in one place. For several years he would bring the ball to Royals games, both here and in spring training, filling up the sides with players he had missed.
George Brett signed — in blue, between Lonnie Smith and Iorg, the most recent addition to the ball — in 2010. Darryl Motley, who homered in Game 7 and caught the final out in right field, signed between Pat Sheridan and Mike Jones.
Howser, who died from a brain tumor in 1987, signed on the sweet spot. The autograph of closer Dan Quisenberry, who also died of brain cancer, in 1998, is also on the ball. “He was very accessible and very friendly,” Greg Dustman said.
Dustman’s ball has 30 signatures, and just one significant player has eluded him: Onix Concepcion, a shortstop who scored the tying run in Game 6 and played only once the rest of his career. The Royals believe he lives in Florida, said Curt Nelson, the director of the team’s Hall of Fame, but little else is known about him.
“He’s never been to any of the reunion events, and I haven’t gone to any great lengths,” Greg Dustman said. “I’m not going to mail the ball unsecured. It means a lot to me.”
Greg Dustman attended the Royals’ wild-card victory over Oakland on Sept. 30, and called it the most exciting game he had seen since 1985. He had tickets for the rainout on Monday and hopes to take his children to the World Series, as his parents did with him. He has signed up for a chance to buy tickets in St. Louis, too.
And if the Royals won another championship, would Dustman start a quest for another signed baseball of champions?
“I sure would like to,” he said.

GREENBURGH, N.Y. — Cam Talbot grew up a Montreal Canadiens fan, watching every move of his idol, Patrick Roy. As a backup to Henrik Lundqvist this season, he has relished a front-row seat to goaltending greatness.
Talbot, a 26-year-old rookie from Caledonia, Ontario, also played an important role in eradicating the hex on the Rangers at Bell Centre in Montreal. He recorded his first N.H.L. shutout with
a 1-0 victory
Nov. 16, which snapped a 0-7-1 streak the Rangers had endured in Montreal since the 2008-9 season. It also was the first Rangers shutout in Montreal since 1967.
Talbot also played the regular-season finale in Montreal, which the Canadiens
won, 1-0, in overtime
.
Talbot does not take credit for banishing the Rangers’ gremlins in Montreal.
“I wouldn’t say it was a jinx,” he said. “But I think it gives everyone a little bit more confidence in that building to win a game or two. Now we we’re just focused on that first game coming up and getting that first win.”
Lundqvist has been spectacular in winning consecutive seven-game series in the playoffs, and Talbot deflected the notion he could have another chance against the Canadiens.
“I’m just sitting back and enjoying watching Hank play right now,” Talbot said. “What he’s been able to do the last four or five games and carry us forward into the next round, it’s been unbelievable. You never want that situation to come up, but if the opportunity arises, I’ll do my best to be ready.”
Whether he play again this postseason — Talbot relieved Lundqvist for the third period of a Game 6 loss in the first round against Philadelphia — he said his first season has proved highly satisfying while providing a litany of valuable lessons.
“You’re always learning, always trying to get better,” said Talbot, who finished 12-6-1 with three shutouts. “And what better place than to be next to one of the best in the world. My mind-set all season — especially down the stretch when I didn’t start much — was to stay focused because anything can happen.”
Rangers Coach Alain Vigneault, whose first N.H.L. coaching job was with the Canadiens in 1997-98, expressed gratitude that he had two solid goalis ready, adding there was not a grand design over which of them started at Bell Centre this season.
“The foundation of any team is goaltending,” Vigneault said. “It just happened that way that Cam played both games, the 1-0 one that we won and the last game of the year that basically meant nothing to both teams when I just wanted to give Hank some rest.”
Talbot appreciates this year’s magic ride, one that could reach a place Lundqvist has never been — the Stanley Cup finals. Witnessing close up what his current mentor does every day resonates for Talbot.
“You don’t get to the level Hank is at without being competitive, without being the hardest worker,” Talbot said. “Hank absolutely hates losing. You can see the fire in his eyes. That alone drives him to be better. And that’s the single biggest thing that drives me, too.”

The Walmart driver whose truck collided with a van carrying the comedian Tracy Morgan and other performers had not slept for more than 24 hours before the crash, New Jersey prosecutors said on Monday.
Prosecutors in Middlesex County charged the truck driver, Kevin Roper, 35, of Jonesboro, Ga., on Saturday with one count of death by auto and several counts of assault by auto in connection with the pileup early that day on the northbound New Jersey Turnpike in Cranbury Township, about 45 miles from New York City. One comedian, James McNair, known as Jimmy Mack, was killed, and Mr. Morgan was critically injured.
In a criminal complaint released on Monday, prosecutors said that at the time of the crash, Mr. Roper had been operating the tractor-trailer “without having slept for a period in excess of 24 hours resulting in a motor vehicle accident.” In a statement issued on Monday, a Walmart spokeswoman, Brooke Buchanan, emphasized that the company believed Mr. Roper “was operating within the federal hours of service regulations,” which limit work shifts to 14 hours, with only 11 of those behind the wheel. She said the company was cooperating with the investigation.
Under New Jersey law
, a driver can be convicted of vehicular homicide if it is shown that he had been without sleep for at least 24 hours when the accident occurred.
A preliminary police investigation found that Mr. Roper had failed to perceive slow-moving traffic ahead of him, and, at the last minute, swerved in an attempt to avoid a collision. The complaint did not explain how the New Jersey State Police determined that Mr. Roper had been sleep deprived.
The crash occurred as Mr. Morgan, 45, a former cast member of “Saturday Night Live” and “30 Rock,” was traveling to New York City from a comedy show in Delaware. Around 1 a.m., a Walmart tractor-trailer collided with the back of the van, a 2012 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter, setting off a chain reaction that involved four other vehicles.
Mr. Morgan sustained injuries including a broken leg, a broken nose and several broken ribs. After the crash, he and his assistant, Jeff Millea, 36, were airlifted to Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital in New Brunswick, N.J. Another comedian, Ardie Fuqua, 43, was also injured.
By Monday, Mr. Morgan was responsive but remained in critical but stable condition. “This recovery will be arduous,” his publicist, Lewis Kay, said in a statement.
The National Transportation Safety Board said Monday that it had sent a team of investigators to New Jersey to focus on the larger issue of the safety of commercial truck operators. The board noted that the number of fatal large truck crashes has steadily risen.
In 2012, there were about 333,000 large truck crashes
, which resulted in 3,921 deaths and more than 104,000 injuries. Of those killed, about 73 percent were occupants of vehicles other than the large truck.
“The upward trend in crashes, fatalities and injuries involving large trucks is a cause for concern,” said the statement, prepared by Don Karol, director of the board’s Office of Highway Safety.
“Too often, responses to our recommendations have been slow or, in some cases, nonexistent,” the statement said. “It should not take additional crashes and loss of life to inspire change.”
Mr. Roper’s next appearance in Middlesex County Superior Court in New Jersey is scheduled Wednesday. He was released Saturday after posting $50,000 bail.

With so many momentum swings, so many spectacular points, so many half chances and incredible shots and ridiculous winners down the line, what ultimately mattered the most in the quarterfinal match between Kei Nishikori and Stan Wawrinka?
The heart of the player is where you start in a battle that lasted 4 hours 15 minutes.
Nishikori
won, 3-6, 7-5, 7-6(7), 6-7(5), 6-4,
but Wawrinka could just have easily done so with a point here, an inch there.
Sitting in the front row on Arthur Ashe Stadium, I got to see up close the incredible firepower of both players. Wawrinka’s raking backhand was good for 17 winners, his forehand crushed 21, and overall he completely dominated with 68 winners to Nishikori’s 41. That doesn’t even begin to tell the story of what happened Wednesday.
In a match that lasted 358 points, the player who won fewer will be moving on. Wawrinka won four more points than Nishikori (181 to 177), or one extra point an hour.
Nishikori won 104 baseline points to Wawrinka’s 96 – another metric of the match that sheds little light on who won and who lost. Wawrinka hit 18 aces to 3, but that turned out to be irrelevant. There were only five breaks of serve in five sets and 15 break points saved as both players battled fatigue and their own personal demons.
Wawrinka won 33 points in the opening set but hitting two huge forehands winners, inside-in down the line, in the second game of the set was all that mattered. The Swiss finished the with an ace down the middle in the ad court to take the early advantage.
Nishikori had five break points in the second set and ultimately converted on one when Wawrinka double faulted at 5-6, 30-40, to level the match. Nishikori had only won 55 percent (6 of 11) of his first serve points in the opening set, but locked down to win 91 percent (20 of 22) in the second set.
The third set was one of the best sets the tournament has seen.
Nishikori stole it, 9-7, in the tiebreaker after failing to convert a set point with Wawrinka serving at 2-5, ad out. Nishikori cooked a forehand down the line into the net that he should have taken cross court.
Nishikori played a horrible game at 5-3, missing a tweener off a lob at 15-30 with Wawrinka standing behind his own baseline. It should have been a forehand, but showtime unfortunately took over.
Wawrinka had another break point at 5-5, 30-40, but pushed a wide backhand into the net from very deep behind the baseline. It was one of the big questions of the match: why did Wawrinka play so deep against an opponent he had to attack?
Wawrinka by 5-3 in the tiebreaker and then by 7-6 to serve for the set. But Nishikori stepped up with an insane backhand winner down the line that should only be attempted once every 100 years. Wawrinka missed a backhand return long on the next point and Nishikori had stolen the third set.
The fourth set was an emotional letdown for the players after such a spectacular third, and they motored along to an eventual tiebreaker with only one break-point opportunity for the set. Wawrinka raced to a 4-1 lead in the tiebreaker before closing it out, 7-5, when Nishikori netted a backhand return on set point.
The fifth set was similar to the fourth, and Nishikori finally broke with Wawrinka serving at 4-5, 30-40.
Matches like these come along once in a while. The winner moves on, and you wish the loser could as well.

Shen Yongping was given a year in prison after making “A Hundred Years of Constitutionalism.”
A Chinese filmmaker who made a documentary on the Chinese Constitution and efforts to get the ruling Communist Party and the government to abide by constitutional law was sentenced on Tuesday by a Beijing district court to one year in prison for running an
“illegal business,”
his lawyer said.
The filmmaker, Shen Yongping, was detained in April and formally arrested on June 4, the 25th anniversary of the military crackdown on student-led protesters in 1989. Many Chinese liberals were detained around around that time this year, and most have since been released.
The court hearing for Mr. Shen began on Dec. 12. In a telephone interview, his lawyer, Zhang Xuezhong, called the verdict and sentencing “nonsense” and said Mr. Shen had not made his documentary, titled “A Hundred Years of Constitutionalism,” for profit. He said Mr. Shen had posted the video online to be downloaded for free and had given away hundreds of DVDs to people who had contributed money for the documentary’s production.
Mr. Shen has been kept in a detention center in the Chaoyang district of Beijing, and Mr. Zhang said he was likely to remain there. If officials count his one-year sentence as having started with his detention in April, then he could be released in four months, Mr. Zhang said.
After Xi Jinping assumed power in November 2012, as the Communist Party chief and later the nation’s president, the authorities began a crackdown on liberal Chinese advocating constitutional rule. People’s Daily, the main party newspaper, published editorials criticizing any such calls. Lately, party leaders have been saying China should be governed according to constitutional law, but there have been no noticeable moves to enforce the Constitution.
Kiki Zhao contributed research.

A federal judge in New York has ruled against
Sirius XM
over an obscure copyright issue that has galvanized the music industry: royalties for recordings made before 1972.
Sirius XM and
Pandora Media
have both been hit in the last year by a series of lawsuits over old recordings. Neither company pays record labels or performing artists on songs recorded before 1972, when federal copyright protection was first applied to recordings. (Both services, however, pay separate royalties for songwriting.)
Last year, members of the 1960s band the Turtles — who sang hits like “Happy Together” and “She’d Rather Be With Me” — sued Sirius XM in California, New York and Florida, saying that by playing its songs without permission, the broadcaster had infringed on the group’s rights under state laws.
The Turtles sought class-action status and asked for $100 million in damages. But these cases may well have broader implications if they lead to changes in copyright law.
On Friday, Judge Colleen McMahon of United States District Court in Manhattan rejected Sirius XM’s motion for summary judgment, saying the Turtles have performing rights to their recordings under New York State law. Sirius XM has until Dec. 5 to dispute remaining facts in the case, the judge wrote, otherwise Sirius XM will be ruled liable for infringement.
“In short, general principles of common law copyright dictate that public performance rights in pre-1972 sound recordings do exist,” Judge McMahon wrote. A representative of Sirius XM declined on Sunday to comment on the decision.
The ruling comes after a separate win for the Turtles in September, when a federal judge in California found Sirius XM liable for infringement under state laws there. That decision was viewed as a major victory for artists and record companies, although its wider impact was unclear because it applied only to California.
Judge McMahon’s decision bolstered the music industry’s position that old recordings are covered under state laws. But both recording and broadcasting executives say the potential for wide confusion over music licensing — for example, it may mean that thousands of AM-FM radio stations, as well as restaurants or sports arenas where music is performed, may have been infringing on recording rights for decades — may require clarification from Congress.
The cases also come as record sales have continued to decline and the music industry has become more reliant on income from online and streaming audio services. SoundExchange, a nonprofit organization that collects recording royalties from Internet and satellite radio, estimates that about $60 million is lost each year in uncollected royalties from oldies.

Earlier this year, a legislator in
Iowa
floated a bill to lower the age at which children can legally shoot handguns. While anyone 20 or younger must be under the direct supervision of a parent or instructor to practice with a pistol or revolver, current state law prohibits children younger than 14 from handgun use, even with a parent around. Rep. Joe Riding, a Democrat from
Altoona
, wanted to lower that to 12.
“If a parent wants to involve their youngster in an activity they love, there’s no reason why they should not involve their 6-year-old daughter or their 9- or 10-year-old daughter,”
Riding told the Des Moines Register
, adding that he taught his own daughter to shoot when she was 9.
The law didn’t pass. Riding said the bill would have sailed through if the
Iowa Gun Owners
lobby hadn’t pushed an amendment to remove age restrictions altogether. But more than that, the effort publicized the minimum shooting age for handguns, which most gun ranges were not enforcing. Now, children under 14 are being barred from shooting handguns at ranges across the state, even when supervised by adults.
Natalie Gibson, 8, who has been shooting with her father since she was 5, was recently sent away from the Polk City range, where she had been practicing with her Walther P22 handgun. “She was upset because she thought she did something wrong,” her father, Nathan Gibson, said. “I had to explain to both my daughters what had happened and why.”
But some Iowans don’t think a shooting range is any place for a child.
“We should teach them ways to solve conflicts that don’t involve guns,” said Kathleen Adams, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who specializes in children and adolescents. She fears that teaching kids handgun shooting gives them the O.K. to use a gun whenever they perceive a situation to be dangerous, even when a parent is not around. “It’s really important for kids to have confidence that their world is safe and that the adults in their world are going to keep them safe,” she said.

Andrew Ross Sorkin, financial columnist for The Times, co-anchor of CNBC’s “Squawk Box” and the author of “Too Big to Fail,” wrote this week’s cover story about the plan by Bill Gates to introduce a new kind of history classes into high schools across the country.
What were you most surprised by when you met Gates in person to discuss this project? Had you reported about him or interviewed him before?
With Gates, I always marvel at the details he has at the tip of his tongue about everything. It is shocking how deep he can go on so many topics. I’ve interviewed him before but not for anything like this piece.
Does Gates see this as relating to his other philanthropy or as totally separate?
I think Gates sees this project as within the framework of his overall philanthropy but a little bit as a one-off. It’s something that he seemed to connect with on a very visceral level.
David Christian, an academic from Australia, accepted Gates’s offer to make over his course for high schoolers. Did he have any concerns or reservations that he expressed to you? How does he think the initiative is going so far?
No reservations. He was thrilled. I’m pretty convinced that Big History would have likely grown pretty large on its own — the approach has support within many corners of academia — but Gates’s involvement is a huge accelerant. I think he’s very pleased about its progress. For a teacher to see a class he invented become this large is quite an accomplishment.
Are there any other courses offered at high schools that are financed by philanthropists? You attended a class at a public school, where a science teacher suggested the Big History course. Is Gates legally allowed to offer financing for such a course at a public school if a teacher doesn’t introduce it in this more “grassroots” fashion? Are other philanthropists following his lead to suggest courses in, say, engineering or more obviously workplace-oriented skills?
As far as I know, there is no single class on a national level, in both public and private schools, being funded by a philanthropist this way. Of course, there are lots of philanthropists who support specific schools and specific programs at certain schools, but nothing this expansive. As for your legal question, the course materials are offered for free to all schools, public and private. Gates doesn’t fund the schools themselves. At the moment, all schools offer the class on a voluntary basis, but it is possible in the future it could become required by certain districts if it becomes popular enough.
You talked to several critics of the course, including Diane Ravitch and Randi Weingarten. Did critics in general oppose the specifics of the course — that it was too science-oriented for a history class — or the principle of a billionaire buying a stake in public-school curricula?
My sense of most of the criticism is that it has less to do with the class itself and more to do with the questions that some critics raise about the power and influence of big money in education. That’s probably inevitable. And when you’re as big a figure as Bill Gates, it is a constant. He clearly upset a large swath of teachers with the Common Core. The question is whether that skepticism will carry over to other educational programs he supports.
The course seems to rely on technology, and you mention the Brooklyn classroom using iPads. Will the class be available in or adapted to less affluent areas that might not have access to technology? Has the demand been higher so far in public schools or charter schools?
The class is built to work in a high-tech and low-tech way. Some schools have iPads. But the curriculum was built to be accessible, so a paper-based version is available as well. So far, both the mix of public-private schools and affluent versus less affluent is pretty balanced.

In
a news conference
at Yankee Stadium in September, baseball’s commissioner,
Bud Selig
, acknowledged that the ever-increasing average length of a game had become a problem worth tackling.
“We have a lot of 2 hours and 30, 2:35, 2:40 games lately; it’s been remarkable,” Selig said. “Then we get a clunker that goes, for whatever reason, three hours and something.”
Selig announced that a committee would look at the rules of the game in hopes of improving the pace, and this season’s playoffs, while unquestionably exciting, are proving the need for change.
From an extraordinary number of extra-inning games to numerous pitching changes to long commercial breaks, a sport that is hoping to get its average duration below three hours instead pushed past that in all 10 games through Saturday. If a game longer than three hours is a clunker, Selig has to be frustrated with an average postseason game time of 4 hours 5 minutes.
In the American League, where three of five games have gone to extra innings, the average sits right at four hours. In the National League, an 18-inning grudge match between San Francisco and Washington on Saturday went nearly six and a half hours, raising the average to 4 hours 10 minutes. Even without that game, the average in the National League would be 3 hours 37 minutes.
Purists will tell you that the playoffs are a different animal, and that the thrilling nature of Kansas City’s recent run of extra-inning victories has made the extra length worth it. The high number of extra-inning games could also be fairly called anomalous. But the slowed-down pace of playoff games, combined with late starting times, have games ending after midnight on the East Coast, which is not ideal for a sport hoping to build its fan base.
To that end,
M.L.B. announced
last week that the committee Selig discussed in September had come up with a series of ways to speed up the game. The changes, ranging from minor to major, will be implemented in the Arizona Fall League.
The changes include barring hitters from stepping completely out of the batter’s box except in certain circumstances; intentional walks no longer requiring any pitches; a maximum break of 2 minutes 5 seconds between innings; a maximum of 2 minutes 30 seconds for pitching changes; and a limit of three timeout conferences covering any meeting involving pitchers and catchers, managers, coaches and batters.
Each of those initiatives could improve the pace, but the sheer number of pitching changes may counteract them. In Game 1 of the division series between St. Louis and the Los Angeles Dodgers, the Cardinals used eight pitchers. St. Louis twice used three pitchers in an inning.
The bigger issue in the postseason is the length of the commercial breaks. The National League wild-card game featured the type of pitching performance that generally results in a short game, with Madison Bumgarner throwing a shutout on 109 pitches against Pittsburgh. Despite that, the game lasted 3 hours 12 minutes.

The 17-year-old from Pennsylvania stood out when he showed up for his freshman year at the University of Arizona, and 50-plus years later, his former classmates remembered him well.
“Looked cool, dressed cool, very preppy,” said Alan Riche, 72, a film producer, thinking back to his new friend in 1959. “We were all wearing those
Peter Gunn
haircuts. The ’60s hadn’t set in yet.”
“Blue blazer,” recalled another classmate, Jeffrey Minker, 72, a lawyer. “Penny loafers. Always dressed well. Very verbal, very funny, very bright. His father supposedly owned a lot of apartment houses and he lived at a place called Dove Lake.”
Dove Lake. The way the new boy talked about that place — the family estate, the servants. “Dove Lake!” said another classmate, Ron Briskman, 73, a former voiceover actor. “He could describe that place down to the last duck. He just made it sound so beautiful, so magnificent.”
The boy from Dove Lake was Michael Forman. Watch his future flit past like pages in a skimmed book:
After that year, he would go home for the summer and never return. Sixteen years later, he would fatally shoot a woman and go to prison in New York. He would be released, only to return, caught in one scheme or another or stealing from girlfriends, charging tens of thousands of dollars to their credit cards.
Mr. Forman was arrested in Manhattan this year and charged with taking money from a friend on the false pretense of securing a SoHo apartment. Today, Mr. Forman is in a jail in Brooklyn on a parole violation stemming from that case. He turned 73 there in May.
His old classmates noticed
a recent column about him
and reached out to share their memories of that 17-year-old whose antics that year, when one flips ahead in the book, now make sense.
He seemed so worldly, with his creased pants and his cigars. “He’d say, ‘Let’s go get a shave,’ ” Mr. Briskman said. “ ‘You haven’t had a shave in a barber shop? You’ve got to!’ ”
One day, young Mr. Forman approached with excitement. “He convinced me he had a friend at the greyhound dog track,” Mr. Briskman recalled. “The race was fixed, and he had an inside track to who would win.” It was a sure thing, and Mr. Briskman said he handed over $20.
“I remember this so well,” Mr. Briskman continued. “He said, ‘The money will be in the left-hand top drawer of your desk.’ I couldn’t wait to open up that drawer.”
But when he did, there was just a note with an expletive and the words, “I lost all the money.”
Don’t worry, Mr. Forman said, we’ll get it back, and he took more money, and more, Mr. Briskman said, until it was all gone.
“I had to drive 120 miles to my parents in Phoenix and walk in the door with my tail deeply embedded between my legs and tell my father I lost the tuition money at the greyhound tracks,” he said.
At the end of the semester, the two friends drove to a drugstore with a good lunch counter. On the way, Mr. Forman asked Mr. Briskman to stop at another store so he could cash a check. He did, and they arrived at their destination and sat.

“There’s a tap on my shoulder,” Mr. Briskman said. “I turn around, and there’s a policeman. ‘Are you Michael Forman?’ ”
Both young men were arrested, Mr. Briskman said, for writing a bad check. The charges against Mr. Briskman were soon dropped.
Mr. Forman went home and never returned. Another classmate, Mr. Minker, made plans to spend the summer with Mr. Forman in Pennsylvania while attending a college summer program, and couldn’t wait to see Dove Lake. He was surprised to find himself in Bala Cynwyd, a nearby town with no lake to speak of.
“It was upper-middle class, but it wasn’t the wealth Michael told us,” he said. “He forgot to tell his parents he invited someone to spend the summer.”
Five decades later, Mr. Forman sat one afternoon last month in jail in Brooklyn and, alternately amused and irritated, listened to a reporter share these accounts. Nonsense, he said: There was no fixed race at the track.
But true: “I was arrested for writing one bad check,” he said, but there was no dramatic lunch-counter scene.
He brushed off the stories, and the larceny charges he faces in Manhattan, as lies.
“People believe the fantasies they tell about themselves,” he said.

I rarely go to the market with a blank slate. Some notion of the ultimate goal — dinner — informs my shopping. Nonetheless, I frequently let the market guide me; dinner is not a rigid “paint by numbers” affair, even if I plan a particular dish. It’s more like a pencil sketch, with some elements that may be erased and redrawn, the way a chef comes up with a daily special.
If you start to approach meal planning this way, thinking first about ingredients that may inspire you and gathering what’s best even if it means making changes on the spot, you’ll wind up with better quality. You will need to make a few basic decisions along the way: how to cook the ingredient, how to season it and how to serve it. Be fearless and let experience steer you. Doing so will make you a more accomplished, inspired cook.
To that end, here is how I arrived at a fish dinner for four, to serve with a lovely bottle of slightly off-dry riesling.
I planned on fillets, and when I went to the market, I hoped to find wild striped bass, sablefish or something similar, with the skin on, so I could use my dependable sear-and-roast method. I crisp the skin to a crackle in a pan, and then finish cooking the fillets in the oven. The method also works with meaty, skinless fillets like hake and mahi-mahi.
Asian seasonings would work very nicely with the wine, so I settled on an Asian vegetable ragout. Had I not decided on Asian, I might have done a mix of little potatoes, capers, baby artichokes and herbs in white wine; or a Spanish sauce with bell peppers, smoked paprika, dicings of chorizo, a whiff of saffron and a splash of sherry; or a mixture as Provençal as a Cézanne, with tomato, fennel, olives, garlic, orange zest and white wine. Most proteins will welcome all sorts of sides. It’s up to you to select what looks best in the market, or even items you have on hand. To make your life less complicated, consider selecting ingredients you already know how to cook.
Asian flavors demand ginger and garlic, bolstered by onions and celery. Those were cooked until tender. Shiitake mushrooms added meatiness. I plundered the pantry for staples like soy sauce, rice vinegar and Chinese five-spice powder, with its anise edge. Fish sauce and oyster sauce also raised their hands, but I did not call on them this time; the sauce was richly saline enough. White wine or dry sherry would be good choices to moisten the mixture, but I decided on beer instead, since its bitterness would tame the salt.
As I cooked, I seasoned little by little, tasting all the while. Do not minimize the importance of tasting, even when you are following exact measurements in a recipe. Feel free to adjust to your own palate. The same goes, to a certain extent, for texture. Time and temperature are flexible components, not rigid rules, and require monitoring.
Though Chinese stir-fries are often thickened with a slurry of cornstarch, I prefer to use miso, which I always keep on hand in the refrigerator. It’s even a wonderful addition to non-Asian dishes, like stews and pot roasts, to thicken the sauce and add nuanced depth. A slick of sesame oil enriched the sauce and burnished the fish.
A handful of bright scallions and cilantro leaves was all it took to finish it.
And, because I never want to lose a successful recipe, I wrote everything down as I went along.

WUPPERTAL, Germany — The stage is full of enormous cacti. A couple in head-to-toe leopard-skin outfits, cat-ears perched on their heads, wander around with beatific, fixed smiles. Punk-rock music pounds.
That music is a tribal beating of drums and a summons to the world of Pina Bausch and her 1987 dance “Ahnen,” newly revived by her company, the Tanztheater Wuppertal, after a decade-long absence from the repertory.
When Bausch died suddenly in 2009, few people would have predicted that five years on, her company would not only still be in demand, but more popular than ever. The performance on Monday night at the opera house here was packed with audience members from all over Europe as well as locals.
Aside from touring extensively and performing Bausch’s work at home, the Tanztheater Wuppertal is currently hosting an ambitious 40th anniversary season that has included revivals like “Ahnen” and an early Stravinsky program, “Frühlingsopfer,” as well as a program of talks, concerts, exhibitions and performances. (A Bausch archive is in the works too.)
Bausch’s posthumous fame is no doubt due in part to the Academy Award-nominated Wim Wenders film, “Pina,” released two years after the choreographer’s death. But it is also testament to the addictive nature of her oeuvre. Once you have seen a few Bausch pieces, you are likely to have been drawn into a theatrical universe that is like no other — immediately, compellingly familiar, no matter how strange the antics onstage. Wildly different in their particularity, the works are alike in a broader way. All are about love, loss, longing and desire, and the ineradicable human will to survive all.
“Ahnen” (a German word meaning either “ancestors” or “foreboding”) is nonetheless on the darker end of the Bausch spectrum. It shares something of its mordant mood with “Viktor,” the work that Bausch created the previous year, and in which the stage is turned into a giant grave. The visual metaphor isn’t quite so stark in “Ahnen”; here, Peter Pabst’s set gives a thorny, desert-scape.
As in “Viktor,” the people who populate this inhospitable environment seem impervious or resigned to its dangers. They also seem mostly impervious to one another. The individuals or couples who briefly come to the fore to speak, dance, gesture, or simply sit silently, all seem marooned in a private reality.
A woman with a heart drawn on her face, silently grinds soap to a powder, staring impassively at the audience. A man with a tutu around his head is transformed into a chieftain, sitting quietly against a cactus for much of the piece. A solitary woman, in dark glasses and pearls, slowly eats a meal and reads letters at one side of the stage. Occasionally she pulls out a gun. Once, late in the work, she shoots, scattering a crowd that has briefly been dancing in unison.
Those unison moments are few, and as with the gunshot, dispelled by violence. Yet this is not, like Bausch’s later pieces, a work of solo dances, or indeed much dancing at all. (A few, spare solos show characteristic, beautifully elaborate, curving arms and pliable bending torsos.) Nor is there much talking. There is a great deal of silence and stillness in “Ahnen”; people seem to be waiting, carrying out tasks — stacking bricks, drilling, rolling up string into a ball, eating, smoking, jumping through a hoop — without much hope that these actions mean, or will amount to, anything at all.

But there is also a dark, brooding humor that leavens the despondency. Dominique Mercy and Nazareth Panadero, two of the 1987 cast members, take turns miming inventive means of faux-mutilating one another. Lutz Förster, a member of the original production (and now the company director), gives a dry translation into German of the aria, “L’Amour est un oiseau rebelle” from Bizet’s “Carmen,” as Mr. Mercy quietly sings. Later Mr. Förster performs a quietly amusing Fred Astaire routine.
The extraordinary thing is how these apparently arbitrary events — conflated, juxtaposed, left in isolation — gradually accrue to create a specific world. Toward the end of “Ahnen,” as in many Bausch pieces, the opening sequences are repeated. There’s no particular message or meaning to extract, yet the images and associations evoked are unforgettable. The life cycle repeats.
Unless, as in Bausch’s “Orpheus and Eurydice,” death brings an end to all. That work, currently being performed by the Paris Opera Ballet, is from an even earlier part of Bausch’s career. Choreographed in 1975, it is a pure-dance piece set to Gluck’s 1762 opera of the same name, with onstage singers who double alongside the dancers in the principal roles.
It’s fascinating to see how strongly Bausch’s choreography is influenced here by her early years studying in New York. Elements of the dance styles and aesthetics of Martha Graham (deep, curving bends of the legs and torso), Antony Tudor (big jumps constrained by arms at the sides of the body) and George Balanchine. This was especially clear in the references to “Serenade” in the beautiful female dance of the third section, “Peace,” fused into a spare physicality in which the singers are effortlessly part of the stage action.
Florian Magnenet, new to the role of Orpheus this season, was slightly muted against Alice Renavand’s passionate Eurydice, but individual roles seem less important here than the dramatic impact of the whole. The score, beautifully performed by the Balthasar-Neumann Ensemble and Chorus, the minimal lines and stark colors of Rolf Borzik’s set, and the architectural groupings of the ensemble make “Orpheus” the purest of theatrical pleasures.

I often make the classic Basque
pipérade
, eggs scrambled with
stewed peppers and tomatoes
. This time, I kept it a little simpler and used my roasted peppers to fill an omelet. I added chopped, fresh herbs and a little bit of Parmesan to the mix. If your peppers are already roasted (I had plenty on hand as I’d been working with roasted peppers all week) this is a 2- to 5-minute dinner. As always, the better the eggs (farm-fresh, pastured), the better the omelet.
Time:
5 minutes
For each omelet:
About 1/3 cup chopped or sliced
roasted peppers
(about 3 ounces)
Salt and freshly ground pepper
2 to 3 teaspoons chopped fresh parsley, thyme, marjoram or basil (optional)
2 large or extra-large eggs
Salt and freshly ground pepper
2 teaspoons milk (optional)
2 teaspoons extra virgin olive oil
2 teaspoons freshly grated Parmesan
1. Make sure peppers are nicely seasoned. Stir in chopped herbs if using.
2. Break eggs into a bowl and beat with a fork or a whisk until frothy. Whisk in salt and pepper to taste and milk if desired.
3. Heat an 8-inch nonstick omelet pan over medium-high heat. Add olive oil. When oil feels hot when you hold your hand above it, pour eggs into the middle of the pan, scraping every last bit into the pan with a rubber spatula. Swirl pan to distribute eggs evenly over the surface. Shake pan gently, tilting it slightly with one hand while lifting up the edges of the omelet with the spatula in your other, to let eggs run underneath during the first minute of cooking.
4. As soon as a few layers of egg are set on the bottom, spoon peppers down the middle of the egg “pancake” and sprinkle on Parmesan. Jerk pan quickly away from you then back toward you so the omelet folds over on itself. If you don’t like your omelet runny in the middle, jerk pan again so omelet folds over once more. Cook for up to a minute longer. Tilt pan and roll out onto a plate.
Yield:
1 serving
Advance preparation:
Roasted and stewed peppers will keep for 3 or 4 days in the refrigerator.
Nutritional information per serving:
263 calories; 17 grams fat; 5 grams saturated fat; 1 gram polyunsaturated fat; 11 grams monounsaturated fat; 375 milligrams cholesterol; 6 grams carbohydrates; 2 grams dietary fiber; 197 milligrams sodium (does not include salt to taste); 15 grams protein

On a recent Saturday night, the place was mobbed. Every table was taken and it was standing room only in the bar and lounge. It made perfect sense; there’s a lot to like at
Bay Kitchen Bar
in East Hampton.
Situated on the top floor of
the Harbor Marina,
the three-month-old restaurant provides unobstructed views of Three Mile Harbor and of fabulous sunsets.
A better reason to visit Bay Kitchen Bar, though less obvious than the dramatic coastal vistas, is the delicious food. Eric Miller, the chef and owner, was the chef and owner of Madison and Main in Sag Harbor last year (it has since closed) and is a co-owner of
two catering
companies
in East Hampton.
Bay Kitchen Bar has the open, airy Hamptons look down pat. The dining porch features open windows fitted with clear plastic flaps that can be lowered if the night turns chilly, along with a white wainscot ceiling and ceiling fans. A sharp royal blue and white color scheme is found throughout the restaurant. Even on that busy Saturday, servers were attentive and delivered the food with efficiency, partly because of the cordiality on the floor; I heard plenty of pleases and thank-yous between waiters, hosts and busboys, which set a nice tone.
Two dishes listed as small plates got raves of “best ever” from our crew. The crab and fish cakes starring fluke, scallops and crab had very little filler and were generously sized. They rested on a marvelous roasted corn and avocado salsa. Even better was the gigantic lobster roll, a toasted brioche roll piled high with big chunks of sweet, tender lobster. The menu said it was freshly shucked, and it tasted like it.
Other appetizer hits were tasty tomato braised meatballs stuffed with sheep’s milk cheese, and ceviche with tuna and crab tossed with heirloom tomatoes and avocado “cooked” with lime juice. The outstanding fisherman’s soup, a mahogany-colored stew with fluke, striped bass and tuna, came with Parmesan and aioli toast floating on top. One diner at the table said he’d love to have quarts of it in his freezer for quick go-to meals on cold nights.
We were less taken with the summer vegetable salad, which was overwhelmed by cauliflower of all colors. The roasted beet, fennel and frisée salad with a wedge of aged goat’s milk feta, all in a citrus Champagne vinaigrette, was better.
Good entree picks were the roasted cod fillet atop a mélange of spring vegetables, baby clams and cannellini beans, and pan-roasted striped sea bass with broccoli rabe, kale and fingerling potatoes. Both fish were lightly cooked and flaky. Handmade spaghetti with an array of baby clams in their shells came tossed in an olive oil sauce with fresh tomatoes, herbs and lardons of smoked pork. I liked the dish, but some of the other entree choices, like the flaky fish and chips and tender Eastern whole belly clams, which both came with a memorable tartar sauce, overshadowed it.
Save room for the house-made desserts. One night Mr. Miller was in the dining room, chatting with guests. When he came to our table, he extolled the virtues of the panna cotta, claiming that it was a healthy choice because it was made from Greek yogurt, local honey and fresh blackberries. Healthy or not, it was delicious. The Key lime tart also proved more than worthy with its soaring toasted French meringue topper. Enjoyable, too, was the crème brûlée, which was served wrapped in crunchy shredded phyllo. The strawberry shortcake had lots of fans at our table, but I thought it could have had more whipped cream. (Is there ever enough whipped cream?)
Still, not much else is lacking at Bay Kitchen Bar. And don’t the crowds know it.

To call Twitch.tv a happy accident would be a grand understatement.
The website has quickly emerged as the go-to destination for watching video games, drawing tens of millions of viewers each month. On Monday, that success led to a huge payday for the company’s founders, as Amazon said it had
reached a deal to buy Twitch
for more than $1 billion.
But Twitch was never supposed to exist.
The site grew from a small side project started by a handful of start-up engineers into a company that — as one of the founders described in an interview last week — happened to land at the right place at the right time.
“It became the tail that wagged the dog,” Emmett Shear, one of Twitch’s founders, said in the interview. “It ended up taking over our whole company.”
In 2006, Mr. Shear and Justin Kan had a question: What would happen if they wore cameras 24 hours a day and broadcast their lives to the web?
That curiosity
led them to create Justin.tv
, and Mr. Kan became the star, “lifecasting” his daily activities for anyone to see. Regular users were invited to do the same.
But Mr. Kan and Mr. Shear quickly noticed that most of Justin.tv’s success came from video game players who used the site to stream themselves playing. In 2011, the group decided to create a separate company, introducing Twitch — a new, entirely gaming-focused version of the site — at the E3 gaming exposition in California.
“It became clear that it was its own beast,” Mr. Shear said.
The company said on Tuesday that Mr. Shear was not available to discuss the company’s plans now that it will be owned by Amazon. But one thing is clear: Twitch is a huge business, a hot spot for people to watch and chat about what has essentially become online gaming as spectator sport, one played not with shoulder pads and helmets, but with ergonomic keyboards and screen-mounted webcams.
The site has many similarities to YouTube, the reigning king of online video. As on YouTube, people host their own individual video channels. Anyone can start a channel, and most anyone can watch others’ channels.
But unlike YouTube, Twitch’s focus is on games and especially on live-streaming video, not recorded video. People with a channel on Twitch host live video sessions of the games they are playing — be it short, first-person shoot-’em-up battles or lengthy group quests in role-playing games like World of Warcraft. Broadcasters often converse with their followers in a dedicated chat room. Popular streamers can amass thousands of followers; the most popular streamers have fans that number in the millions.
In part, Mr. Shear said, Twitch’s surge in popularity is the result of technological changes beyond the company’s control. Live-streamed video is only as good as the Internet network it runs on. And until recent years, the broadband backbone in the United States struggled to handle the heavy traffic that live streaming demands.
“This couldn’t have existed five years before we launched it,” Mr. Shear said. “You needed high-resolution video. You needed broadband Internet, which just wasn’t there.”

South Korea, by comparison, has had more robust Internet networks than the United States for years. When the service was becoming popular with gamers, United States broadband speeds were a fraction of those in South Korea, according to a
2010 report from Akamai
, an Internet content delivery network. High-speed access was also more expensive in the United States than in South Korea and other countries, according to Akamai.
It is perhaps no surprise, then, that South Korea has been the leader in live-streamed gaming, hosting major “e-sports” tournaments in which gamers compete against one another in front of millions of online viewers for big prizes — essentially Seoul’s version of Monday Night Football.
But now in the United States and elsewhere, Mr. Shear said, “Internet access is just getting cheaper and cheaper, faster and faster.”
The speed has helped the site generate 55 million regular visitors from around the world each month, and those people watch 16 billion minutes of its videos. More than 1.1 million people broadcast their gaming activity to the service. (In the meantime, Justin.tv operations were
wound down completely
this month.)
Along with the advancement of technology, Twitch largely credits its success to its robust network of engaged members. In essence, the company has turned into a cluster of ad hoc social networks, a place to chat about anything from the game on the screen to what people had for breakfast that morning.
“Every channel is its own microcommunity, where everyone gets to know each other over their shared interests,” Mr. Shear said.
Tessa Brook, a 30-year-old woman who goes by the name Tessachka on Twitch, posts her regular online gaming schedule — about 42 hours a week — so her 5,000 followers know when they can watch her play.
“I think Twitch was born out of a simple need to share game experiences,” said Brian Blau, a technology analyst at Gartner Research. Twitch is not a traditional social media company, like Facebook, he said, but the site’s social aspect is at its core. “Twitch connects gamers together with social-like features, and that creates a community.”
For Ms. Brook and popular streamers like her, gaming can also be lucrative. Popular players who are selected for Twitch’s “partner” program earn a cut of the revenue from advertisements that run on their channel. Streamers can also accept monetary donations of a dollar or more from viewers.
Mr. Shear said the next generation of Twitch gamers could be players of more casual games, like those popular on smartphones. Clash of Clans, for example, one of the most popular smartphone games, is becoming particularly popular to stream, he said.
But Mr. Shear said that the company was focused on more than smartphones. He said the company would also most likely pursue international expansion, especially in fast-growing regions like South America.
“Mobile is going up, adoption of every new generation of gaming console is going up, and there’s more money being spent on PC gaming than ever before,” Mr. Shear said. “Gaming, as a whole, is growing.”
Timothy D. Cook, Apple’s chief executive, introduced a smartwatch, a wearable device that combines health and fitness tracking with communications.

A
Vatican
investigation of American nuns begun under the previous pope, prompting protests from outraged Catholics, ended in Rome on Tuesday with the release of a generally appreciative report that acknowledged the achievements and the challenges the nuns face given their dwindling ranks.
The relatively warm tone in
the report
, and at the
Vatican
news conference that released it, were a far cry from six years ago when the investigation was announced, creating fear, anger and mistrust among women in religious communities and convents across the United States.
“Sorry, folks. This is not a controversial document,” Mother M. Clare Millea, an American nun who directed the investigation, said at the news conference. Instead, she said, it was “a challenge for all of us.”
If anything, the report may help spur the process of including women in more decision-making roles in church life, some church observers said. According to the report, some nuns felt that bishops and priests did not welcome their opinions on “pastoral decisions which affect them or about which they have considerable experience and expertise.”
The report concluded by citing Pope Francis’ call “to create still broader opportunities for a more incisive female presence in the church.” But it did not make any concrete suggestions.
Pope Francis, who was elected last year and had no role in initiating the investigation, celebrated Mass on Tuesday with some of the nuns and clergymen who carried it out.
Mother Millea said that Francis told them he knew the investigation was an “arduous experience,” and said of the nuns in the United States, “Please give them all my blessing.”
But the American sisters are not out from under Vatican scrutiny yet. There is still a separate review of the
Leadership Conference of Women Religious
, an umbrella group representing about 80 percent of American nuns. The Vatican’s doctrinal office
accused that group
of hosting speakers and issuing materials that had a feminist cast and strayed from Catholic doctrine. In 2012, the Leadership Conference was put under the oversight of an American bishop for a thorough overhaul — a process that was supposed to last five years.

Sister Sharon Holland, the president of the Leadership Conference, who spoke at the Vatican news conference on Tuesday, said in an interview afterward that her organization had been working “very well” with the overseer bishop and his team, and that the oversight may end sooner than five years. She said there may be a news conference soon to discuss the outcome.
She also had an upbeat take on the new Vatican report, saying in the news conference: “It is not a document of blame or simplistic solutions. One can read the text and feel appreciated and trusted to carry on.”
The investigation, known as an apostolic visitation, was initiated in 2008 under Pope Benedict XVI with only a vague explanation. The Vatican said it was the largest apostolic visitation ever undertaken in a single country.
Cardinal Franc Rodé
, the head of the Vatican office for religious orders, said then that the purpose was to examine “the quality of life of religious women in the United States.”
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
The Vatican usually orders an apostolic visitation in the case of a serious problem or scandal, but there was no clear event or cause in this situation.
Cardinal Rodé later said he was concerned about “a certain secular mentality that has spread in these religious families and, perhaps, also a certain feminist spirit.”
About 350 communities of religious women were sent questionnaires asking about such things as their numbers and mission, prayer schedules, living arrangements, financial assets and property. Nearly 80 investigators visited 90 communities of nuns.
Some religious communities took umbrage at the investigation and did not cooperate fully. A few nuns said in interviews that their communities had decided to give the Vatican only a copy of their original founding constitutions. The survey questions about property and finances led some nuns to suspect that the Vatican could be assessing their communities’ assets with an eye to appropriating them. The nuns were eventually told that they did not have to answer the questions about finances, but the suspicions never fully faded.
The report acknowledged the resistance, saying that the Vatican was “well aware that the apostolic visitation was met with apprehension and suspicion by some women religious,” and that “the lack of full cooperation was a painful disappointment for us.”
Other communities of nuns, however, did cooperate and said that the process was an opportunity to reflect on their lives and communities and to be in more direct communication with the wider church.
Mother Agnes Mary Donovan, coordinator of the Council of Major Superiors of Women Religious, a smaller and more conservative umbrella group of nuns, said at the news conference that the visitation was “an overwhelmingly beautiful experience.”
If the Vatican does reprimand any communities or call for any changes, that would be done in private. Cardinal João Braz de Aviz, a Brazilian who succeeded Cardinal Rodé as head, said his office will send “individual reports” to some communities of nuns that “may have been the object of some concerns.”
But the broad report released Tuesday contained only brief, muted criticism, saying that the communities should “carefully review their spiritual practices and ministry to assure that these are in harmony with Catholic teaching.”
The concerns of some nuns that the Vatican had wanted the sisters to shift away from “social justice” ministry or advocacy were allayed by the report. Instead, it encouraged them to continue working with the poor and toward “the elimination of the structural causes of poverty.”
But the picture the report presented of the women’s orders was grim. It found that there were now about 50,000 nuns in the United States, a decline of 125,000 from the peak in the mid-1960s. The median age of American nuns is now in the mid- to late 70s, according to figures reported in other studies.
Many communities of nuns also struggled financially, “despite careful stewardship,” the report found. The sisters work for free or are “undercompensated,” sometimes in church positions. With the church downsizing, some had been laid off.
The investigators found that “many sisters expressed great concern” about how to continue their religious orders’ purpose and mission and the lack of a new generation to provide leadership. Many orders have invested a lot of time and energy in initiatives to attract new members. But the report found that “the results are not commensurate with the expectations and efforts.”
The two Vatican investigations had caused an uproar among some Catholics who picketed in front of parishes and cathedrals across the country. Nearly 60,000 signed a petition of support for the nuns, which was delivered to the American bishops at their conference in Atlanta in 2012. Several prominent bishops said at that meeting that the two crackdowns on the nuns had been damaging to the church’s public relations.
The Nun Justice Project, a coalition of Catholic groups organized to defend the sisters, on Tuesday called the visitation process “demeaning and a huge waste of time” that diverted the sisters from vital work.
